## One dataset, start to finish

Two printed reference works, the *Colonial Office List* (1862–1966) and the *India Office List* (1886–1947), carry a terse biography for every senior official: born, schooled, every posting, every honour. The same man recurs in forty annual editions. The OCR garbles a name here and there. Two men who share a surname threaten to collapse into one career.

Over a few months, one historian with a coding agent turned those volumes into a knowledge graph and an [animated atlas](https://jimclifford.ca/col_matching/) of imperial careers:

| | Colonial Office List | India Office List |
|---|---|---|
| Person records within each List | 27,526 | 19,400 |
| Career events | 180,470 | 124,694 |
| Events located to a Wikidata place | 131,343 | 80,238 |

The hour is about how, and about where in that process a historian has to decide something. The two person counts are resolved within each List; their sum is a roster count, not a count of unique people across both services.

By the end you will have marked up an entry, judged a proposed record and an identity match, and decided how to preserve a disagreement between sources. We work on a shared example in a browser; the final step takes the method to your own material.

## Three questions

Technical terms are explained where they first appear on each page, and in the [glossary](glossary.qmd).

A historian turning a text into data asks three questions of it, and each has a decision the historian must own. Models and scripts carry those decisions across the collection; their output still needs review.

| | The question | The model does | You decide |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Structure** | What is a record here? | Proposes the fields, fills them for 65,000 entries, reports what it could not parse | What counts as an event; whether the record changed the meaning |
| **Clean** | Is this one person or two? | Clusters the candidates, argues each case, keeps the evidence | Merge, keep apart, or leave for review |
| **Ground** | Which place, which person, in the shared vocabulary? | Retrieves candidates with evidence | Supported, unresolved, or wrong |

## The second half of the method

Extraction is half of it. The other half is looking at the result in a form where errors are visible. The atlas was built to answer a research question, and it turned out to be the best error detector the project had. A British Columbia premier appearing in Australia, a cluster of South African postings landing at Harare, two nodes both called Baluchistan: each was seen on the map, traced to a rule, fixed in the pipeline, and re-emitted for everyone it affected. Build, extract, visualise, see, fix, rerun. That loop is what the hour demonstrates.

## The hour

| Minutes | | |
|---|---|---|
| 0–7 | [The atlas](steps/01-atlas.qmd) | The video; then one man's entry turned into identifiers, coordinates and arcs, and the corrections carried through to the rebuilt atlas |
| 7–13 | [The source](steps/02-source.qmd) | One printed entry. Mark up what you would extract |
| 13–23 | [Structure](steps/03-structure.qmd) | Raw OCR, the discussion with Claude Code, why Python rules alone were insufficient, and the hybrid workflow |
| 23–30 | [Clean](steps/04-identity.qmd) | Forty editions, one person: the merge rules and the cases that need a historian |
| 30–40 | [Ground](steps/05-ground.qmd) | A live Wikidata lookup, and a chatbot asked to do the same from memory |
| 40–46 | [The map finds the errors](steps/06-loop.qmd) | Brewster: the wrong place, then an unsupported appointment |
| 46–56 | [Exercise](review/index.html) | Three decisions with reasons; five further cases to take home |
| 56–60 | [Your own data](steps/07-your-data.qmd) | Taking the three questions to another collection |

## What you need

A browser. The [decision exercise](review/index.html) and the [mark-up exercise](annotate/index.html) run from saved results and need no account or key. Remote participants have the same pages; each exercise has a button that copies a one-line summary of your work for the Zoom chat. There is a [two-page printable handout](handout.pdf) with Balmer and the same three decisions for the room.

## Further
